{{Short description|Theorem in quantum information theory}}

In quantum information and computation, the '''Solovay–Kitaev theorem''' says that if a set of single-[[qubit]] [[quantum gate]]s generates a [[Dense subset|dense]] [[subgroup]] of [[SU(2)]], then that set can be used to approximate any desired quantum gate with a short sequence of gates that can also be found efficiently. This theorem is considered one of the most significant results in the field of [[Quantum computing|quantum computation]] and was first announced by [[Robert M. Solovay]] in 1995 and independently proven by [[Alexei Kitaev]] in 1997.<ref name="KY97">{{Cite journal|last=Kitaev|first=A Yu|date=1997-12-31|title=Quantum computations: algorithms and error correction|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1070/rm1997v052n06abeh002155|journal=Russian Mathematical Surveys|volume=52|issue=6|pages=1191–1249|doi=10.1070/rm1997v052n06abeh002155|bibcode=1997RuMaS..52.1191K |s2cid=250816585 |issn=0036-0279|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Kitaev|first1=Alexei Yu.|title=Classical and quantum computation|last2=Shen|first2=Alexander|last3=Vyalyi|first3=Mikhail N.|publisher=American Mathematical Society|year=2002|isbn=0-8218-2161-X|location=Providence, Rhode Island|oclc=48965167}}</ref> [[Michael Nielsen]] and Christopher M. Dawson have noted its importance in the field.<ref name="DN06">{{Cite journal|last1=Dawson|first1=Christopher M.|last2=Nielsen|first2=Michael|date=2006-01-01|title=The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm|url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/2011679.2011685|journal=Quantum Information & Computation|volume=6|pages=81–95|doi=10.26421/QIC6.1-6|language=EN|arxiv=quant-ph/0505030}}</ref>

A consequence of this theorem is that a quantum circuit of <math>m</math> constant-qubit gates can be approximated to <math>\varepsilon</math> error (in [[operator norm]]) by a quantum circuit of <math>O(m\log^c(m/\varepsilon))</math> gates from a desired finite [[Quantum logic gate#Universal quantum gates|universal gate set]] (where c is a constant).<ref>{{Cite book|chapter=The Solovay–Kitaev theorem|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/quantum-computation-and-quantum-information/solovaykitaev-theorem/0087DB96E95447C2C6B1C1F61F14D642|last1=Nielsen|first1=Michael A.|last2=Chuang|first2=Isaac L.|date=2010|title=Quantum Computation and Quantum Information: 10th Anniversary Edition|pages=617–624|language=en|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511976667.019|isbn=9780511976667|access-date=2020-05-20}}</ref> By comparison, just knowing that a gate set is universal only implies that constant-qubit gates can be approximated by a finite circuit from the gate set, with no bound on its length. So, the Solovay–Kitaev theorem shows that this approximation can be made surprisingly ''efficient'', thereby justifying that quantum computers need only implement a finite number of gates to gain the full power of quantum computation.

== Statement ==
Let <math>\mathcal{G}</math> be a finite set of elements in [[SU(2)]] containing its own inverses (so <math>g \in \mathcal{G}</math> implies <math>g^{-1} \in \mathcal{G}</math>) and such that the group <math> \langle \mathcal{G} \rangle </math> they generate is dense in  SU(2). Consider some <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>. Then there is a constant <math>c</math> such that for any <math>U \in \mathrm{SU}(2)</math>, there is a sequence <math>S</math> of gates from <math>\mathcal{G}</math> of length <math>O(\log^c(1/\varepsilon))</math> such that <math>\|S - U\| \leq \varepsilon</math>. That is, <math>S</math> approximates <math>U</math> to operator norm error.<ref name="DN06" /> Furthermore, there is an efficient algorithm to find such a sequence.  More generally, the theorem also holds in [[Special unitary group|SU(d)]] for any fixed d.

This theorem also holds without the assumption that <math>\mathcal{G}</math> contains its own inverses, although presently with a larger value of <math>c</math> that also increases with the dimension <math>d</math>.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Bouland |first1=Adam |title=Efficient Universal Quantum Compilation: An Inverse-free Solovay-Kitaev Algorithm |date=2021-12-03 |arxiv=2112.02040 |last2=Giurgica-Tiron |first2=Tudor}}</ref>

== Quantitative bounds ==
The constant <math>c</math> can be made to be <math>\log_{(1+\sqrt{5})/2} 2 + \delta = 1.44042\ldots + \delta</math> for any fixed <math>\delta > 0</math>.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |mode=cs2 |last=Kuperberg |first=Greg |title=Breaking the cubic barrier in the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm |date=2023-06-22 |class=quant-ph |eprint=2306.13158}}</ref> However, there exist particular gate sets for which we can take <math>c=1</math>, which makes the length of the gate sequence optimal up to a constant factor.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ross|first1=Neil J.|last2=Selinger|first2=Peter|title=Optimal ancilla-free Clifford+T approximation of z-rotations|url=https://www.rintonpress.com/journals/doi/QIC16.11-12-1.html|journal=Quantum Information & Computation|date=2016 |volume=16|issue=11–12|pages=901–953|doi=10.26421/QIC16.11-12-1|arxiv=1403.2975
}}</ref> The [[spectral gap conjecture]], if true, would imply that it is possible to take <math>c=1</math> for a generically chosen gate set.

== Proof idea ==

Every known proof of the fully general Solovay–Kitaev theorem proceeds by recursively constructing a gate sequence giving increasingly good approximations to <math>U \in \operatorname{SU}(2)</math>.<ref name="DN06" /> Suppose we have an approximation <math>U_{n-1} \in \operatorname{SU}(2)</math> such that <math>\| U - U_{n-1} \| \leq \varepsilon_{n-1}</math>. Our goal is to find a sequence of gates approximating <math>U U_{n-1}^{-1}</math> to <math>\varepsilon_n</math> error, for <math>\varepsilon_n < \varepsilon_{n-1}</math>. By concatenating this sequence of gates with <math>U_{n-1}</math>, we get a sequence of gates <math>U_n</math> such that <math>\|U - U_n\| \leq \varepsilon_n</math>.

The main idea in the original argument of Solovay and Kitaev is that commutators of elements close to the identity can be approximated "better-than-expected". Specifically, for <math>V,W \in \operatorname{SU}(2)</math> satisfying <math>\|V - I\| \leq \delta_1</math> and <math>\|W - I\| \leq \delta_1</math> and approximations <math>\tilde{V}, \tilde{W} \in \operatorname{SU}(2)</math> satisfying <math>\|V - \tilde{V}\| \leq \delta_2</math> and <math>\|W - \tilde{W}\| \leq \delta_2</math>, then

:<math>\|VWV^{-1}W^{-1} - \tilde{V}\tilde{W}\tilde{V}^{-1}\tilde{W}^{-1}\| \leq O(\delta_1\delta_2),</math>

where the [[big O notation]] hides higher-order terms. One can naively bound the above expression to be <math>O(\delta_2)</math>, but the group commutator structure creates substantial error cancellation.

We can use this observation to approximate <math>U U_{n-1}^{-1}</math> as a group commutator <math>V_{n-1}W_{n-1}V_{n-1}^{-1}W_{n-1}^{-1}</math>. This can be done such that both <math>V_{n-1}</math> and <math>W_{n-1}</math> are close to the identity (since <math>\|U U_{n-1}^{-1} - I\| \leq \varepsilon_{n-1}</math>). So, if we recursively compute gate sequences approximating <math>V_{n-1}</math> and <math>W_{n-1}</math> to <math>\varepsilon_{n-1}</math> error, we get a gate sequence approximating <math>U U_{n-1}^{-1}</math> to the desired better precision <math>\varepsilon_n</math> with  <math>\varepsilon_n</math>. We can get a base case approximation with constant <math>\varepsilon_0</math> with an exhaustive search of bounded-length gate sequences.

== Proof of Solovay-Kitaev Theorem ==

Let us choose the initial value <math>\varepsilon_0</math> so that  <math>\varepsilon_0 < \varepsilon'</math> to be able to apply the iterated “shrinking” lemma. In addition we want <math>s\varepsilon_0 < 1</math> to make sure that <math>\varepsilon_k</math> decreases as we increase <math>k</math>. Moreover, we also make sure that <math>\varepsilon_0</math> is small enough so that <math>\varepsilon_k^{2} < \varepsilon_{k+1}</math>.

Since <math>\langle G \rangle</math> is dense in <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)</math>, we can choose <math>l_0</math> large enough<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kitaev |first1=Yu |title=Quantum computations: algorithms and error correction |url=http://mi.mathnet.ru/eng/umn/v52/i6/p53}}</ref> so that <math>G^{l_0}</math> is an <math>\varepsilon_0^2</math>-net for <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)</math> (and hence for <math>\operatorname{S}_{\varepsilon_0}</math>, as well), no matter how small <math>\varepsilon_0</math> is. Thus, given any <math>U \in \operatorname{SU}(2)</math>, we can choose <math>U_0 \in G^{l_0}</math> such that <math>|| U - U_0|| < \varepsilon_0^2</math>. Let <math>\Delta := UU_0^{+}</math> be the “difference” of <math>U</math> and <math>U_0</math>. Then
:<math>\|\Delta_1 - I\| = \|(U - U_0)U_0^+\| =  \|U - U_0\|< \varepsilon_0^2<\varepsilon_1.</math>

Hence, <math>\Delta_1\in \operatorname{S_{\varepsilon_1}}</math>. By invoking the iterated "shrinking" lemma with <math>k = 1</math>, there
exists <math>U_1 \in G^{l_1}</math> such that
:<math>\|\Delta_1 - U_1\| = \|U U_0^+ - U_1\| =  \|U - U_1 U_0\|< \varepsilon_1^2.</math>

Similarly let <math>\Delta_2:=\Delta_1 U_1^+ = U U_0^+ U_1^+</math>. Then 
:<math>\|\Delta_2 - I\| = \|(U - U_1 U_0)U_0^+ U_1^+\| =  \|U - U_1 U_0\|< \varepsilon_1^2<\varepsilon_2.</math>

Thus, <math>\Delta_2\in \operatorname{S_{\varepsilon_2}}</math> and we can invoke the iterated "shrinking" lemma (with
<math>k = 2</math> this time) to get <math>U_2 \in G^{l_2}</math> such that <math>\|\Delta_2 - U_2\| = \|U U_0^+ U_1^+ - U_2\| =  \|U - U_2 U_1 U_0\|< \varepsilon_2^2.</math>

If we continue in this way, after k steps we get <math>U_k \in \operatorname{G}^{l_k}</math> such that
:<math>\|U - U_k U_{k-1} ... U_0\|< \varepsilon_k^2.</math>

Thus, we have obtained a sequence of
:<math>L=\sum_{m=0}^kl_m=\sum_{m=0}^k5^m l_0=\frac{5^{k+1}-1}{4}l_0 < \frac{5}{4}5^kl_0
</math>

gates that approximates <math>U</math> to accuracy <math>\varepsilon_k^2</math>. To determine the value of <math>k</math>, we set <math>\varepsilon_k^2 = \left((s\varepsilon_0 )^{(3/2)^k}/s\right)^2=\varepsilon</math>
and solve for k:

:<math>\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^k =\frac{\text{log}(1/s^2 \varepsilon)}{2\text{log}(1/s\varepsilon_0)}
.</math>

Now we can always choose <math>\varepsilon_0</math> slightly smaller so that the obtained value
of <math>k</math> is an integer.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Nielsen, Chuang |first1=M.A., I.L. |title=Quantum Computation and Quantum Information (Cambridge University Press, 2000), Appendix 3, pp. 617{624.}}</ref> Let <math>c=\text{log}5/\text{log}(3/2) \approx 3.97</math> so that<math>5^k = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{kc}</math>. Then

:<math>L<\frac{5}{4}5^kl_0=\frac{5}{4}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{kc}l_0=\frac{5}{4}\left(\frac{\text{log}(1/s^2 \varepsilon)}{2\text{log}(1/s\varepsilon_0)}\right)^cl_0
</math>
Hence for any <math>U \in \operatorname{SU}(2)</math> there is a sequence of <math>L=O(\text{log}^c(1/\varepsilon))</math> gates that
approximates <math>U</math> to accuracy <math>\varepsilon</math>.

== Solovay-Kitaev algorithm for qubits ==

Here the main ideas that are used in the SK algorithm have been presented. The SK algorithm may be expressed in nine lines of pseudocode. Each of these
lines are explained in detail below, but present it here in its entirety both for the reader's reference, and to stress the conceptual simplicity of the algorithm:

 '''function''' Solovay-Kitaev(Gate <math>U</math>, depth <math>n</math>) '''is'''
 
     '''if''' (<math>n</math> == 0)
 
         '''return''' Basic Approximation to <math>U</math>
 
     '''else'''
 
         '''set''' <math>U_{n-1}</math> = Solovay-Kitaev(<math>U</math>,<math>n-1</math>)
 
         '''set''' <math>V,W</math> = GC-Decompose(<math>UU_{n-1}^+</math>)
 
         '''set''' <math>V_{n-1}</math> = Solovay-Kitaev(<math>V,n-1</math>)
 
         '''set''' <math>W_{n-1}</math> = Solovay-Kitaev(<math>W,n-1</math>)
 
         '''return''' <math>U_n=V_{n-1}W_{n-1}V_{n-1}^+W_{n-1}^+U_{n-1}</math>;
         
 '''end function'''

Let us examine each of these lines in detail. The first line:

 '''function''' Solovay-Kitaev(Gate <math>U</math>, depth <math>n</math>) is

indicates that the algorithm is a function with two inputs: an arbitrary single-qubit quantum
gate, <math>U</math>, which we desire to approximate, and a non-negative integer, <math>n</math>, which controls
the accuracy of the approximation. The function returns a sequence of instructions which
approximates <math>U</math> to an accuracy <math>\varepsilon_n</math>, where <math>\varepsilon_n</math> is a decreasing function of <math>n</math>, so that as <math>n</math> gets
larger, the accuracy gets better, with <math>\varepsilon_n\to 0</math> as <math>n\to \infty</math>. <math>\varepsilon_n</math> is described in detail below.

The <code>Solovay-Kitaev</code> function is recursive, so that to obtain an <math>\varepsilon_n</math>-approximation to <math>U</math>,
it will call itself to obtain <math>\varepsilon_{n-1}</math>-approximations to certain unitaries. The recursion terminates
at <math>n=0</math>, beyond which no further recursive calls are made:

 '''if''' (<math>n</math> == 0)
  
     '''return''' Basic Approximation to <math>U</math>

In order to implement this step it is assumed that a preprocessing stage has been completed
which allows one to find a basic <math>\varepsilon_0</math>-approximation to arbitrary <math>U \in \operatorname{SU}(2)</math>. Since <math>\varepsilon_0</math> is a constant, in principle this preprocessing stage may be accomplished simply by enumerating
and storing a large number of instruction sequences from <math>G</math>, say up to some sufficiently large
(but fixed) length <math>l_0</math>, and then providing a lookup routine which, given <math>U</math>, returns the closest sequence.

At higher levels of recursion, to find an <math>\varepsilon_n</math>-approximation to <math>U</math>, one begins by finding an
<math>\varepsilon_{n-1}</math>-approximation to <math>U</math>:

 '''else'''
 
     '''set''' <math>U_{n-1}</math> = Solovay-Kitaev(<math>U</math>,<math>n-1</math>)

<math>U_{n-1}</math> is used as a step towards finding an improved approximation to <math>U</math>. Defining <math>\Delta</math>≡ <math>UU^+_{n-1}</math>, the next three steps of the algorithm aim to find an <math>\varepsilon_{n}</math>-approximation to <math>\Delta</math>, where <math>\varepsilon_{n}</math> is some improved level of accuracy, i.e., <math>\varepsilon_{n}<\varepsilon_{n-1}</math>. Finding such an approximation
also enables us to obtain an <math>\varepsilon_{n}</math>-approximation to <math>U</math>, simply by concatenating exact
sequence of instructions for <math>U_{n-1}</math> with <math>\varepsilon_{n}</math>-approximating sequence for <math>\Delta</math>.

How do we find such an approximation to? First, observe that <math>\Delta</math> is within a distance <math>\varepsilon_{n-1}</math> of the identity. This follows from the definition of <math>\Delta</math> and the fact that <math>U_{n-1}</math> is within a distance <math>\varepsilon_{n-1}</math> of <math>U</math>.

Second, decompose <math>\Delta</math> as a group commutator <math>\Delta = VWV^+W^+</math> of unitary gates <math>V</math> and <math>W</math>. For any <math>\Delta</math> it turns out that this is not obvious and that there is always an infinite set of
choices for <math>V</math> and <math>W</math> such that <math>\Delta = VWV^+W^+</math>. For our purposes it is important that we
find <math>V</math> and <math>W</math> such that <math>d(I, V ), d(I,W) < c_{gc}\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n-1}}</math> for some constant <math>c_{gc}</math>. We call such a decomposition a ''balanced group commutator''.

 '''set''' <math>V,W</math> = GC-Decompose(<math>UU_{n-1}^+</math>)

For practical implementations we will see below that it is useful to have <math>c_{gc}</math> as small as
possible.

The next step is to find instruction sequences which are <math>\varepsilon_{n-1}</math>-approximations to <math>V</math> and <math>W</math>:

 '''set''' <math>V_{n-1}</math> = Solovay-Kitaev(<math>V,n-1</math>) 
 
 '''set''' <math>W_{n-1}</math> = Solovay-Kitaev(<math>W,n-1</math>)

The group commutator of <math>V_{n-1}</math> and <math>W_{n}</math> turns out to be an <math>\varepsilon_{n-1}</math> ≡ <math>c_{\text{approx}}\varepsilon_{n-1}^{3/2}</math>-approximation to <math>\Delta</math>, for some small constant <math>c_{\text{approx}}</math>. Provided <math>\varepsilon_{n-1}<1/c_{\text{approx}}^2</math>, we see that <math>\varepsilon_n<\varepsilon_{n-1}</math>, and this procedure therefore provides an improved
approximation to <math>\Delta</math>, and thus to <math>U</math>.

The constant <math>c_{\text{approx}}</math> is important as it determines the precision <math>\varepsilon_0</math> required of the initial approximations. In particular, we see that for this construction to guarantee that <math>\varepsilon_0>\varepsilon_1>...</math> we must have <math>\varepsilon_0<1/c_{\text{approx}}^2</math>.

The algorithm concludes by returning the sequences approximating the group commutator, as well as <math>U_{n-1}</math>:

 '''return''' <math>U_n=V_{n-1}W_{n-1}V_{n-1}^+W_{n-1}^+U_{n-1}</math>;

Summing up, the function <code>Solovay-Kitaev(U, n)</code> returns a sequence which provides an <math>\varepsilon_n=c_{\text{approx}}\varepsilon_{n-1}^{3/2}</math>-approximation to the desired unitary <math>U</math> . The five constituents in this sequence
are all obtained by calling the function at the <math>n-1</math>th level of recursion.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=CHRISTOPHER M. DAWSON |first1=MICHAEL A. NIELSEN |title=THE SOLOVAY-KITAEV ALGORITHM |date=2005 |eprint=quant-ph/0505030 }}</ref>
